notice: Comparison drills: sets of terms CISSP likes to blur, each with short scenarios where you pick the term that fits. Original content.

drills.title: BCP vs DRP vs incident response

items.name: BCP
items.meaning: Keeps critical business processes running through a disruption; business-wide.

items.name: DRP
items.meaning: Restores IT systems and data after a disruption; technology-focused.

items.name: IR
items.meaning: Detects, contains and eradicates security incidents and learns from them.

prompts.text: Branch staff switch to paper forms while the core banking system is down.
prompts.why: Keeping the business process going by other means is continuity.

prompts.text: The database is restored at the recovery site from last night's backup.
prompts.why: Restoring systems and data is disaster recovery.

prompts.text: An analyst isolates a host showing ransomware behaviour and preserves its memory.
prompts.why: Containment and evidence handling are incident response.

prompts.text: Management decides which business processes must resume within four hours.
prompts.why: Prioritising business processes and tolerances is continuity planning.

prompts.text: Engineers fail over the email service to the secondary data centre.
prompts.why: Recovering a technology service at another site is disaster recovery.

prompts.text: After a phishing compromise, the team writes a lessons-learned report.
prompts.why: Post-incident review is part of the incident response lifecycle.

drills.title: Who secures it: IaaS, PaaS or SaaS customer?

items.name: IaaS
items.meaning: Customer secures the guest OS and everything above it.

items.name: PaaS
items.meaning: Customer secures the application code, data, identities and configuration.

items.name: SaaS
items.meaning: Customer secures its data, user access and the service's settings.

prompts.text: The customer must patch the Linux kernel on its cloud servers.
prompts.why: Only in IaaS does the customer manage the operating system.

prompts.text: The customer deploys code to a managed app platform and must fix its own vulnerable library.
prompts.why: In PaaS the provider runs the platform; the code and its dependencies are the customer's.

prompts.text: The customer's only duties for its email service are user access, MFA and sharing settings.
prompts.why: In SaaS the customer manages data, identities and configuration.

prompts.text: The customer configures host firewalls on the virtual machines it built.
prompts.why: Guest OS firewalls belong to the customer in IaaS.

prompts.text: The customer sets which external users may access shared folders in a file-sharing service.
prompts.why: Sharing configuration is the SaaS customer's responsibility.

prompts.text: The customer chooses runtime settings and secrets for its managed database-backed web app.
prompts.why: Application configuration and secrets are the PaaS customer's.

drills.title: Control types: preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, compensating

items.name: Preventive
items.meaning: Stops an incident from happening.

items.name: Detective
items.meaning: Finds an incident during or after it happens.

items.name: Corrective
items.meaning: Fixes the cause or the damage after an incident.

items.name: Deterrent
items.meaning: Discourages an attacker from trying.

items.name: Compensating
items.meaning: An alternative used when the preferred control is not feasible.

prompts.text: A firewall rule blocks inbound SMB from the internet.
prompts.why: It stops the traffic before harm can occur.

prompts.text: A SIEM alert fires when an account logs in from two countries within an hour.
prompts.why: It identifies a likely incident as it happens.

prompts.text: After malware is found, the endpoint is reimaged from a clean build.
prompts.why: It removes the cause and returns the system to a good state.

prompts.text: A login banner warns that all access is monitored and misuse will be prosecuted.
prompts.why: It discourages misuse but blocks nothing.

prompts.text: A legacy system cannot support MFA, so it is placed behind a jump host that requires MFA.
prompts.why: It substitutes for a control the system cannot provide.

prompts.text: Daily review of privileged account activity by a second administrator.
prompts.why: Reviews find misuse after it happens.

prompts.text: Applying a vendor patch that closes a vulnerability exploited last week.
prompts.why: It fixes the weakness that was exploited.

items.name: Symmetric
items.meaning: One shared secret key encrypts and decrypts; fast; suits bulk data. AES, ChaCha20.

items.name: Asymmetric
items.meaning: Public and private key pair; slow; suits key exchange and signatures. RSA, ECC, ML-KEM, ML-DSA.

items.name: Hashing
items.meaning: One-way fixed-length digest; no key; shows whether data changed. SHA-256, SHA-3.

prompts.text: Encrypting a 2 TB database backup quickly before it goes offsite.
prompts.why: Bulk data needs a fast cipher such as AES.

prompts.text: Two parties agree a session key over the internet with no shared secret.
prompts.why: Key exchange without a shared secret is what public-key cryptography solves.

prompts.text: Checking that a downloaded installer matches the vendor's published fingerprint.
prompts.why: Comparing digests shows whether the file changed.

prompts.text: A supplier signs an invoice so the buyer can prove who sent it.
prompts.why: Digital signatures use a private key to sign and a public key to verify.

prompts.text: Storing user passwords so the system never keeps the passwords themselves.
prompts.why: Passwords are stored as salted, slow hashes, not encrypted.

prompts.text: Full-disk encryption on staff laptops.
prompts.why: Disk encryption uses a symmetric cipher such as AES-XTS.

drills.title: Data roles: owner, processor, custodian, subject

items.name: Owner / controller
items.meaning: Decides why and how data is processed; accountable; sets classification.

items.name: Processor
items.meaning: Processes data on the controller's behalf and instructions.

items.name: Custodian
items.meaning: Implements and operates the protection day to day: backups, access, patching.

items.name: Data subject
items.meaning: The individual the personal data is about.

prompts.text: The HR director decides which salary fields are Confidential.
prompts.why: Setting classification and purpose belongs to the owner.

prompts.text: A payroll bureau runs payslips exactly as the employer instructs.
prompts.why: It acts on the controller's instructions.

prompts.text: The DBA restores the HR database from last night's backup.
prompts.why: Day-to-day protection and operation is the custodian's job.

prompts.text: An employee asks to see the personal data the company holds about her.
prompts.why: She is the person the data is about.

prompts.text: A cloud email provider stores mailboxes under a data processing agreement.
prompts.why: It processes data for the customer under contract.

prompts.text: The bank decides to use transaction data for fraud scoring.
prompts.why: Deciding a new purpose is the controller's decision.

drills.title: Data at rest, in transit, in use

items.name: At rest
items.meaning: Stored on disk, tape or in a database.

items.name: In transit
items.meaning: Moving across a network or between systems.

items.name: In use
items.meaning: Being processed in memory or by an application.

prompts.text: A stolen backup tape holds an unencrypted customer database.
prompts.why: Stored data on media is at rest.

prompts.text: An attacker captures traffic on hotel Wi-Fi as a laptop syncs email.
prompts.why: Data moving over a network is in transit.

prompts.text: Malware scrapes card numbers from a payment terminal's memory.
prompts.why: Data being processed in memory is in use.

prompts.text: A file share is protected with full-disk encryption on the server.
prompts.why: Disk encryption protects stored data.

prompts.text: A confidential computing enclave keeps data encrypted while it is processed.
prompts.why: Enclaves protect data during processing.

prompts.text: Replication between data centres runs over an IPsec tunnel.
prompts.why: IPsec protects data moving between sites.

items.name: RPO
items.meaning: How much data loss is tolerable, measured as time back to the last good copy.

items.name: RTO
items.meaning: How long until the system is restored.

items.name: WRT
items.meaning: Time after restore to verify data and resume work.

items.name: MTD
items.meaning: The longest the business can tolerate the process being down. RTO + WRT ≤ MTD.

prompts.text: The business can lose at most 15 minutes of transactions.
prompts.why: It limits data loss, so it drives backup or replication frequency.

prompts.text: Beyond 24 hours down, the regulator would suspend the payment licence.
prompts.why: The point where harm becomes unacceptable is the maximum tolerable downtime.

prompts.text: After the platform is back, reconciling the ledger takes three hours.
prompts.why: Verification and catch-up after restore is work recovery time.

prompts.text: IT commits to having the CRM running again within six hours of a failure.
prompts.why: Time to restore the system is the recovery time objective.

prompts.text: Nightly backups at 02:00 are no longer enough; replication every five minutes is needed.
prompts.why: Backup frequency is set by tolerable data loss.

items.name: Quantitative
items.meaning: Puts money and numbers on risk (SLE, ARO, ALE); supports spending decisions.

items.name: Qualitative
items.meaning: Rates risk by judgement (high, medium, low; heat maps); supports prioritisation.

prompts.text: The CFO asks whether a US$50,000 a year control is worth buying.
prompts.why: A spending decision needs an expected loss in money.

prompts.text: A new team has no loss history and needs to rank 40 risks by next week.
prompts.why: Quick ranking with thin data suits judgement-based ratings.

prompts.text: Experts rate each risk anonymously over several rounds until they converge.
prompts.why: The Delphi technique gathers judgement, not monetary values.

prompts.text: A server worth US$120,000 loses 25% of its value per incident, expected twice a year.
prompts.why: SLE = 30,000; ALE = 60,000: a monetary calculation.

prompts.text: The board wants a one-page heat map of the top ten risks for its meeting.
prompts.why: Heat maps present ratings, not monetary values.

drills.title: Risk treatment: avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept

items.name: Avoid
items.meaning: Stop or never start the activity that creates the risk.

items.name: Mitigate
items.meaning: Reduce likelihood or impact with controls.

items.name: Transfer
items.meaning: Shift part of the impact to another party, such as an insurer or contractor; accountability stays.

items.name: Accept
items.meaning: The owner formally takes on the remaining risk, within appetite and with a review date.

prompts.text: A bank decides not to launch a crypto custody service after assessing the regulatory and theft risk.
prompts.why: Not undertaking the activity removes the risk entirely.

prompts.text: A retailer buys cyber insurance to cover forensic and notification costs after a breach.
prompts.why: Insurance shifts part of the financial impact; the retailer remains accountable.

prompts.text: A hospital adds MFA and EDR to reduce the chance of ransomware spreading.
prompts.why: Controls reduce likelihood and impact.

prompts.text: The risk owner signs off a low-rated risk on a legacy kiosk, with a review in six months.
prompts.why: A documented decision by the owner, within appetite and time-bound.

prompts.text: A telecom outsources its card payments to a PCI-certified gateway so card data never touches its systems.
prompts.why: The gateway carries the card-data handling; the telecom still oversees the supplier.

prompts.text: A company stops letting staff use personal USB drives after repeated malware incidents.
prompts.why: It removes the activity that creates the risk rather than controlling it.

items.name: Clear
items.meaning: Logical overwrite of user-addressable storage; defeats simple recovery tools.

items.name: Purge
items.meaning: Defeats laboratory recovery while leaving the media reusable: sanitise commands, crypto erase, degaussing magnetic media.

items.name: Destroy
items.meaning: Physically destroys the media (IEEE 2883 calls this Destruct): shred, disintegrate, incinerate.

prompts.text: Laptops that held public marketing material are being reused inside the same team.
prompts.why: Low-sensitivity reuse inside the organisation suits clearing.

prompts.text: Self-encrypting SSDs are reassigned to another organisation; their media keys are destroyed.
prompts.why: Cryptographic erase is a purge method that allows reuse.

prompts.text: Drives that held top-secret data reach end of life.
prompts.why: The highest sensitivity at end of life calls for physical destruction.

prompts.text: Magnetic tapes are degaussed before being sold.
prompts.why: Degaussing purges magnetic media.

prompts.text: A failed SSD cannot run its sanitise command but held patient records.
prompts.why: If purge cannot be done, destruction is the safe option.

prompts.text: A file server's volumes are overwritten once before it is redeployed internally.
prompts.why: A single logical overwrite for internal reuse is clearing.

items.name: Bell-LaPadula
items.meaning: Confidentiality: no read up, no write down.

items.name: Biba
items.meaning: Integrity: no read down, no write up.

items.name: Clark-Wilson
items.meaning: Integrity through well-formed transactions, separation of duties and audit.

items.name: Brewer-Nash
items.meaning: Chinese Wall: prevents conflicts of interest based on access history.

prompts.text: A Secret-cleared process may not save its output to an Unclassified folder.
prompts.why: No write down protects confidentiality.

prompts.text: Untrusted field reports may not update the calibration master data.
prompts.why: No write up protects higher-integrity data.

prompts.text: Clerks can change ledger balances only through the approved posting program, never directly.
prompts.why: Well-formed transactions through certified programs.

prompts.text: After working on one airline's file, an analyst is blocked from a rival airline's file.
prompts.why: Access depends on what the analyst has already seen.

prompts.text: A process may not read data at a lower integrity level than its own.
prompts.why: No read down keeps low-integrity data from influencing the subject.

prompts.text: Users cleared Confidential may not open Top Secret files.
prompts.why: No read up is the simple security property.
